slides.headline: One deck, every language
slides.subtitle: Translated words, the same layout
slides.speaker_notes: Welcome everyone. This deck is narrated in English and Hindi.

slides.purpose: Thesis slide introducing the core methodology.
slides.key_message: The core process of multilingual deck creation.
slides.headline: Write, translate, narrate
slides.subtitle: How it works
slides.speaker_notes: First, you write the deck once. Then the words are translated, and the layout stays. Finally, every click step has its own narration.

slides.key_message: The three steps that make the process work.

slides.headline: Layout consistency
slides.subtitle: Structure vs. Content
slides.body: The structure remains fixed while the content is localized.
slides.speaker_notes: The key takeaway here is that the presentation structure is preserved, allowing for easy localization.

slides.key_message: The principle of maintaining layout integrity.
slides.headline: Preserve the layout
slides.subtitle: Core principle

result.title: Database Migrations Explained
result.narrative_arc: Beginning: Introducing the concept of schema changes. Middle: Detailing the role of the migration record. End: Summarizing the process and its importance.

slides.headline: Managing Schema Evolution in Deckastra
slides.subtitle: A guide for new colleagues on how the system tracks changes.
slides.body: Welcome to the team. This presentation outlines the process of database migrations within our system.
bullets: The role of the migration record
slides.code: No code sample required for this introductory slide.
slides.caption: Source: db-guide
slides.speaker_notes: We start by defining what a database migration is in the context of Deckastra. Essentially, it's the structured way we track and apply changes to the underlying database schema over time. This ensures consistency across all environments.

slides.purpose: Turning point: Stating the core function.
slides.key_message: Migrations are the official record of schema changes.
slides.headline: The Migration Record: Schema Change Tracking
slides.eyebrow: The migration record is the source of truth.
slides.subtitle: Every structural update is logged.
slides.body: The core function of a migration is to serve as an immutable log of every schema change applied to the database.
bullets: Provides a history of the database structure.
Acts as the single source of truth for structure.
slides.caption: Source: db-guide
slides.speaker_notes: Think of the migration record as the official ledger for our database structure. It doesn't just show *what* the final state is; it shows *how* we got there. This is crucial for debugging and understanding the evolution of our data models.

slides.key_message: The migration lifecycle in simple steps.
slides.headline: The Migration Process Flow
slides.subtitle: A high-level view of the workflow.
slides.body: The process involves proposing a change, generating the migration artifact, and applying it to the database.
bullets: Apply the artifact to the target database.
The record is updated upon successful application.
slides.quote: The migration record is the source of truth.
slides.caption: Source: db-guide
slides.speaker_notes: When you work on a new feature that requires a database change, you follow this path. The key takeaway here is that the record is updated *after* the change is successfully applied, cementing its role as the historical anchor for our database structure.

slides.purpose: Comparing the concept to a real-world scenario.
slides.headline: Automated vs. Manual Schema Updates
slides.subtitle: The benefit of structured recording.
slides.body: Manual changes are risky; migrations are controlled and traceable.
slides.caption: Source: db-guide
slides.speaker_notes: The biggest win with migrations is control. Instead of developers manually running SQL scripts, we use the migration system. This means every change is versioned, tested, and applied predictably, drastically reducing the risk of human error.

slides.key_message: The fundamental fact of the migration.
slides.headline: The Core Principle of Migration
slides.subtitle: The migration record is the source of truth.
slides.body: This principle is explicitly stated in our documentation.
bullets: The migration record is the source of truth.
slides.caption: Source: db-guide
slides.speaker_notes: This is the single most important sentence for anyone new to the topic. It’s not a suggestion; it’s a fact. When we talk about database structure, the migration record is the definitive, unchangeable history of that structure.

slides.purpose: Showing the structure of the record.
slides.headline: Migration Record Structure
slides.subtitle: A snapshot of the change.
slides.body: The record itself contains metadata about the schema version and the change applied.
slides.caption: Source: db-guide
slides.speaker_notes: This snippet shows you the basic structure of the record. You'll see fields like the schema version and a unique ID. These elements allow us to track exactly which version of the database structure corresponds to which change.

slides.headline: Conclusion: Mastering Database Migrations
slides.subtitle: Your path forward.
slides.body: In summary, migrations provide control, history, and reliability for our database structure.
bullets: The record is the single source of truth.
Always check the migration history before making changes.
slides.quote: Always check the migration history before making changes.
slides.caption: Source: db-guide
slides.speaker_notes: To wrap up: migrations are our disciplined approach to database evolution. They ensure that every structural change is intentional, documented, and reversible. Familiarize yourself with the migration history in every project you touch.

issues.message: The title slide message 'One deck, every language the room speaks' is slightly abstract; while the concept is clear, it could be more direct about the deck's function for the audience (locale, narration, sound test suites).
issues.suggested_fix: Slightly rephrase the subtitle to explicitly mention the audience or the core deliverable.

issues.message: The narrative flow is clear (Write, Translate, Narrate), but the transition between the three steps could be enhanced with stronger visual cues beyond the simple click animations.
issues.suggested_fix: Ensure the visual representation of the three steps is highly distinct and memorable.

result.summary: The deck is well-structured, adheres to the specified technical theme, and maintains strong visual consistency. The narrative clearly outlines the three-step process. The layout is clean and readable, and the motion is used effectively to emphasize key points. It is ready for use.

issues.message: The title slide is too dense with technical jargon and lacks a clear, immediate narrative hook for a new colleague. It needs to immediately establish the 'why' and 'what' in a way that resonates with someone new to the project.
issues.suggested_fix: Simplify the headline to focus on the core value proposition: 'Deckastra: Turning Repositories into Editable Presentations.' The subtitle should then clearly state the main benefit: 'How the document model keeps humans in control of AI edits.'

issues.message: The narrative flow of the architecture slide is purely descriptive of the pipeline. It needs a clearer story about *why* the separation of concerns (e.g., Agent vs. Transaction Service) is critical for maintainability and safety, rather than just listing the steps.
issues.suggested_fix: Frame the 'Agent graph' section around the concept of 'Safety and Reviewability.' Use the diagram to show the flow, but use accompanying text to explicitly state: 'No agent writes directly to the store; every change goes through the transaction service, ensuring a human checkpoint.'

issues.message: The key message 'An agent changes one property, not a whole slide' is good, but the supporting text needs to be more explicit about the technical consequence. It needs to explain *why* this narrow change is reviewable (i.e., it's a targeted operation, not a full document rewrite).
issues.suggested_fix: Expand the caption to explain the mechanism: 'AI edits are scoped to a single property path (e.g., font size), allowing for granular, reviewable patches rather than monolithic document rewrites.'

result.summary: The deck has strong technical content and good visual consistency, but the narrative structure is currently too descriptive rather than persuasive. The story needs to focus on the core value proposition—how the system maintains human control through its architectural separation—to make the concepts immediately understandable and engaging for a new colleague.
